title: Describe a time you drove a technical improvement or migration (e.g., monolith to microservices, Java 8 to 17, on-prem to cloud): what was the plan, the challenges, and the outcome?
shortTitle: Driving a Technical Improvement or Migration: plan, challenges, and outcome
keyPoints: Big migrations succeed by moving incrementally with a fallback, never by a big-bang cutover.
Use the strangler-fig pattern: new system gradually takes over while old runs side by side.
Shift traffic gradually via canary: route a small percentage to new, compare results, increase only when parity is proven.
Name the real challenges: data consistency, behavioral parity, team coordination.
Quantify the outcome: deployment time, failure rate, or performance improvement.
Keep a fallback so you can revert instantly if the new path misbehaves.
The key discipline is verifying parity continuously, not trusting the new system on faith.

s1_definition.oneliner: Big migrations succeed by moving incrementally with a fallback, measuring at each step, and never risking a big-bang cutover.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Incremental, not big-bang** – Migrate piece by piece with the old system running as a fallback.
- **Strangler-fig pattern** – The new system gradually takes over responsibilities from the old one.
- **Canary traffic shifting** – Route a small percentage of real requests to the new system and compare results.
- **Parity verification** – Continuously compare old and new outputs; block rollout if they disagree.
- **Quantified outcome** – Measure deployment time, failure rate, or performance before and after.
- **Fallback always ready** – At any point you can revert to the old system instantly.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India moving from one giant old transfer system to a set of smaller modern services, without ever stopping customer transfers for Rajesh or Priya. Driving a migration is like renovating a bank branch while it stays open: you move one counter at a time, keep the old one running as a fallback, and only close the old counter once the new one proves itself.

sections.s6_takeaway:
At National Bank of India, the transfer logic for Rajesh's and Priya's accounts lived inside a large old monolith that was slow to deploy and risky to change. I drove the migration of that logic into a new dedicated transfer service. The hard part was that this code moves real customer money, so any behavioral difference between old and new could mis-handle a transfer.

My plan was an incremental, strangler-fig migration. I put a router in front that could send a small percentage of real transfers to the new service while the old monolith kept running as a fallback. For every request I ran it through both old and new logic and compared the results, so I could prove the new service produced exactly the same outcomes before relying on it.

The main challenges were behavioral parity and team coordination. When the new service disagreed with the old, the router served the trusted old result and blocked us from increasing the rollout until we fixed the discrepancy. I kept the percentage low until mismatches stayed at zero, then raised it gradually.

The outcome was that we fully migrated the transfer logic with zero customer-facing incidents, and deployment time dropped from hours to minutes. Large migrations succeed not through courage but through discipline: move incrementally, keep a fallback, verify parity continuously.

Remember one sentence: Migrate incrementally with a fallback, verify parity between old and new systems continuously, and only trust the new system once the data proves it behaves identically.
